analysis.one_liner: Bans giant online platforms from favoring their own products over competitors on their platforms.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2026 by six senators from both parties and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it illegal for the largest online platforms — those with over $175 billion in annual revenue reaching a third or more of Americans — to rig their own marketplaces: they could not bury rivals in search results, use sellers' private data to launch competing products, force developers to buy their other services, or block users from changing default settings. Enforcement would sit with the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general, with fines of up to 10% of a company's US revenue and, for repeat offenders, possible forfeiture of executives' pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses and app developers that sell through big platforms, rival companies that compete with platform owners, and consumers who get more choice, fairer search results, and possibly lower prices and fees.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a covered platform from ranking its own products above competitors' products, and from using data generated by sellers on the platform to build competing offerings [S2].
Bans tying — conditioning access to the platform on buying the platform owner's other products or services — and bans impeding business users' access to platform features or their own data [S2].

Lets users change default settings that steer them to the platform owner's products, and lets regulators seek temporary injunctions and civil penalties of 1 to 10 percent of a violator's US revenue [S2].
Requires expedited court handling, aiming for final judgment within a year, and allows state attorneys general to sue on behalf of residents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The giant platform companies — Amazon, Apple, Google, and Meta are the ones that meet the size and reach thresholds — which would face new legal limits, litigation risk, and fines measured against their US revenue; some costs could be passed to users or sellers if compliance changes how free services are run.

drawbacks.text: The bill's bright-line rules apply to fast-changing products, and even with affirmative defenses for privacy, security, and fraud prevention [S2], platforms argue that integrated features like maps inside search or app-store review protect users — loosening them could create real security and privacy risks that courts would have to sort out case by case.

Compliance and litigation under the new rules would impose costs on the platforms, which could show up as changes to free consumer services or higher fees for sellers; the bill also exempts foreign-adversary-controlled businesses from protection, which creates a two-tier rulebook [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real: platform owners today both run the marketplace and compete in it, and this bill directly targets that conflict. The main honest cost is uncertainty — bright-line rules written for today's tech could produce clumsy results or security friction, and enforcement would depend heavily on how courts apply the defenses. On balance, the bill addresses a documented market-power problem, but its practical effect would hinge on the FTC, DOJ, and the courts.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and has seen no hearings, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Senator Grassley introduced the bill on June 10, 2026, joined by Senators Klobuchar, Durbin, Hawley, Whitehouse, and Booker — a bipartisan, six-sponsor introduction [S1].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary; no further action appears in the record [S4].
Five senators — four Democrats and one Republican — are listed as cosponsors alongside Grassley [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The big platform companies, which face no new legal limits while the bill sits without committee action; businesses competing on those platforms gain nothing yet either.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.role: Senate bill sponsor; Chair, Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which he chairs; no committee action has followed.

against.name: Major online platform companies
against.role: Companies that would be covered by the bill
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against earlier versions of this legislation and funded campaigns portraying it as a threat to popular services and user security.

sides.party_line_note: The six initial sponsors split 3 Republicans and 3 Democrats, and the five additional cosponsors are 4 Democrats and 1 Republican; no vote has occurred.

industries.industry: Giant online platforms (Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta)
industries.note: The $175 billion revenue and 34 percent reach thresholds target exactly these companies [S2], and they would face bans on self-preferencing and seller-data use plus fines up to 10 percent of US revenue. The bill's limits are designed to stop practices that cost sellers and consumers money or choice.

industries.industry: App developers and small businesses selling on big platforms
industries.note: These businesses would get fairer search placement, access to platform features on equal terms, portability of their own data, and protection from retaliation for complaining to regulators [S2].

industries.industry: Companies competing against platform owners' products
industries.note: Rivals in search, retail, maps, and apps could no longer be disadvantaged by the platform owner's own competing offerings under the ranking and data prohibitions [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to committee this late in a Congress rarely reach the floor. The bill has no scheduled committee action, and with the session ending in January 2027, the realistic path is that it stalls in the Judiciary Committee unless leadership chooses to prioritize it; if it dies, a similar bill would need to be reintroduced in the next Congress.
